lead: A derivation is the step-by-step rewriting of a string using grammar rules. A parse tree draws the same rewriting as a tree. The tree shows grouping; the derivation shows order. Compilers build trees because the tree is what the next phase needs. This chapter defines both views and connects them.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for grammar notation, and Unit 1 for strings and concatenation.

blocks.text: A context-free grammar has productions such as A → α. A variable (nonterminal) is a symbol that can be replaced. A terminal is a symbol that cannot. A derivation starts from the start symbol S. At each step, choose one variable in the current string and replace it by the right side of one of its productions. The current string is called a sentential form. It may contain both terminals and variables.
u A v ⇒ u α v
blocks.where: u and v are strings of terminals and variables; A is a variable; A → α is a production.

blocks.text: The symbol ⇒ means one rewriting step. The symbol ⇒* means zero or more steps. A derivation of a string w is a chain S ⇒ ... ⇒ w. A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost variable in the sentential form. A rightmost derivation always expands the rightmost variable. For the grammar E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → ( E ) | id, the string E + T has E as its leftmost variable and T as its rightmost variable.

sections.h3: Parse tree: the same rewriting drawn

blocks.text: A parse tree for a grammar G has root S. Each internal node is labeled by a variable A. If the children of that node are labeled X1, X2, ..., Xk from left to right, then A → X1 X2 ... Xk must be a production of G. Leaves are labeled by terminals or by ε. The yield (also called the frontier) is the string of leaf labels read left to right; an ε leaf adds the empty string.

A subtree is a node together with all its descendants. It is itself a parse tree for the variable at that node. The height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from root to a leaf. A tree with one node has height 0.

Theorem: w ∈ L(G) exactly when G has a parse tree with root S and yield w. Matching theorem: every parse tree comes from exactly one leftmost derivation and exactly one rightmost derivation of its yield. The leftmost derivation is forced: at each step the next variable to expand is the leftmost one still present. The rightmost derivation is forced the same way from the right.

The number of derivations of a string grows with the number of variables. Independent variables can be expanded in different orders. All those orders can give the same tree. A parser must recover grouping, not rewriting order. That is why a compiler stores a parse tree or a syntax tree.

In id + id × id, the leftmost derivation takes 8 steps and the rightmost takes 8 steps. Both give one tree. The tree places × below +, so multiplication is done first. A compiler can walk the tree bottom-up: evaluate the two id leaves under ×, multiply them, then add the left id.

To prove ambiguity you need two different parse trees or two different leftmost derivations for the same string. Two ordinary derivations that differ only in the order of independent expansions use the same tree and prove nothing.

figure.caption: The parse tree for id + id × id: variables are circles, terminals are boxes. The × node sits inside the T below the +, so the multiplication is grouped first, and the leaves read left to right give back the string.

examples.question: Grammar: E → E + T | T, T → T × F | F, F → ( E ) | id. (a) Give a leftmost derivation of id + id × id. (b) Give a rightmost derivation. (c) Count the steps in each. (d) Draw the parse tree.
steps: Leftmost derivation: always expand the leftmost variable.
E ⇒ E + T ⇒ T + T ⇒ F + T ⇒ id + T ⇒ id + T × F ⇒ id + F × F ⇒ id + id × F ⇒ id + id × id. Count arrows: 8 steps.
Rightmost derivation: always expand the rightmost variable.
E ⇒ E + T ⇒ E + T × F ⇒ E + T × id ⇒ E + F × id ⇒ E + id × id ⇒ T + id × id ⇒ F + id × id ⇒ id + id × id. Count arrows: 8 steps.
Both derivations produce the same parse tree, shown in the figure after Section 1. Its leaves read id, +, id, ×, id.
examples.answer: The leftmost derivation takes 8 steps; the rightmost derivation takes 8 steps; both give the same parse tree with yield id + id × id.

traps: Reading the tree from the top down as if that were the derivation order. The tree fixes grouping only; the leftmost or rightmost order is a separate choice.
Using two ordinary derivations that differ only in expansion order to claim ambiguity. That proves nothing; compare trees or leftmost derivations.
Calling every sentential form a terminal string. A sentential form may still contain variables; only a yield with no variables is a terminal string.
Confusing height with number of nodes. Height counts edges on the longest root-to-leaf path; a single-node tree has height 0.

quiz.q: Define a sentential form in a derivation.
quiz.a: A string of terminals and variables that appears at some step of a derivation from the start symbol.

quiz.q: Why does a parse tree not record the order of rewriting?
quiz.a: It records only which production is used at each node. Independent branches can be expanded in either order, and the tree is the same.

quiz.q: Grammar S → SS | a. Give a leftmost derivation of aaa and count its steps.
quiz.a: S ⇒ SS ⇒ aS ⇒ aSS ⇒ aaS ⇒ aaa. That is 5 steps.

quiz.q: Grammar E → E + T | T, T → id. Give a leftmost derivation of id + id + id and state the yield.
quiz.a: E ⇒ E + T ⇒ E + T + T ⇒ T + T + T ⇒ id + T + T ⇒ id + id + T ⇒ id + id + id. Yield is id + id + id. That is 6 steps.

quiz.q: A student shows two derivations of one string that differ only in the order of expanding two independent variables. Does this prove ambiguity? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The two derivations have the same parse tree. Ambiguity needs two different parse trees or two different leftmost derivations.

quiz.q: Can a parse tree have an internal node labeled id in this grammar? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Internal nodes are variables. Leaves are terminals; id is a terminal. An internal node labeled id would need a production with id on the left, which a CFG does not allow.

quiz.q: State the theorem that connects L(G) with parse trees.
quiz.a: A string w is in L(G) exactly when G has a parse tree with root S and yield w.

beyond: Not for the exam. Parser generators such as ANTLR and yacc build parse trees or syntax trees from grammar rules. Compilers then lower the tree to an intermediate representation. Modern tools also produce concrete syntax trees that keep comments and spacing for editors. Search for abstract syntax tree, leftmost derivation parser, and Earley parser to go further.
